title: Volkswagen spent £430 million to buy Rolls-Royce but couldn't buy the name
dek: Since the 1971 split, Rolls-Royce's trademark has not belonged to the automaker; Volkswagen spent £430 million buying the factory and Bentley but couldn't acquire the Rolls-Royce name itself, and had to cede it to BMW.
why: An acquisition that seemed winnable with deep pockets lost to a trademark clause buried in a contract 27 years earlier—valuable reference for anyone doing M&A or navigating brand licensing.
who: Professionals focused on M&A negotiations, brand licensing, and trademark clause design; and listeners interested in the history of luxury brands like Rolls-Royce and Bentley.
skip: 0:00-2:00 backstory recap; skip if you've already heard last episode on the Rolls-Royce engine split.

points.h: Bentley's turbo strategy turned it from 5% to 50% of Crewe's production
points.body: Bentley was originally just Rolls-Royce's second-tier badge variant; in 1980, fewer than 5% of Crewe's output carried the Bentley name. David Plastow, who led at the time, spotted Bentley's racing heritage and its distinctly sporty positioning, so he commissioned independent turbocharged models like the Mulsanne Turbo. Within six years by 1989, Bentley's share of Crewe's production had rocketed from 5% to 50%, becoming the company's true profit driver.

points.h: BMW wanted to buy the Rolls-Royce badge to charge luxury prices
points.body: BMW group CEO Pischetsrieder was blunt about it: BMW had the capacity to build a car that matched Rolls-Royce in performance—technology wasn't the issue. The problem was that a BMW badge on the grille couldn't command that price. Swap it for Rolls-Royce and the price could climb to the heavens. BMW had already maxed out the luxury segment; what it needed was an ultra-luxury brand to fill the pricing gap—the core motivation driving its persistence more than Toyota or Ford would have shown.

points.h: Eight days after signing with BMW, Volkswagen outbid it at the airport lounge
points.body: Vickers had accepted BMW's £340 million first and final bid on April 29, 1998—the deal seemed done. Just eight days later, Volkswagen CEO Piëch flew into London's Northolt Airport on a company jet, met Vickers' chief commercial officer face-to-face in the Churchill lounge, and handed over an offer of £430 million—nearly 25% higher. A month later, Vickers' shareholders voted for Volkswagen.

points.h: The Rolls-Royce name and logo stayed with the engine maker, not the automaker
points.body: The crucial clause was buried in the 1971 split: the Rolls-Royce name and the RR logo were permanently kept by Rolls-Royce plc (the aero engine business), merely ‘permanently licensed free of charge’ to the car company—with two veto rights. If the car business sold to a foreign company, or if quality fell below standard, Rolls-Royce plc could revoke the license. Volkswagen got the factory, drawings, the Bentley brand name, and the Spirit of Ecstasy hood ornament, but not the Rolls-Royce name itself.

points.h: The licensing risk was public from the start; Volkswagen did its homework anyway
points.body: Many post-mortems paint Volkswagen as a cash-rich bumbler caught off guard, but the episode notes this risk was always public: when the 1971 agreement was made, the UK government reported it to the EU Commission; in 1991 when Crewe laid off staff, parliament members publicly questioned the trademark clause; and in early 1998, Vickers itself petitioned the EU to abolish both restrictive conditions. VW's executives had also quietly sounded out Rolls-Royce plc's intentions.

points.h: Volkswagen bet on fait accompli, but BMW fought back and won the name
points.body: Piëch's strategy fit his reputation: control the factory, technology, and people first, put the chips on the table, then force Rolls-Royce plc to comply—skip the direct negotiations. But BMW moved fast. It immediately paid £40 million to buy the license to the Rolls-Royce trademark from Rolls-Royce plc, and on July 9 issued notice that one year later it would stop supplying engines to Rolls-Royce cars—cutting off the oxygen.

points.h: Two state premiers settled the split on a golf course in mid-July
points.body: The stalemate lasted until the morning of July 28, when Volkswagen, BMW, and Vickers suddenly signed a memorandum of understanding at a golf course in Germany: Volkswagen kept Crewe and the Bentley brand; BMW took the Rolls-Royce trademark and pledged to build a new factory in the UK; cars built at Crewe during the transition could still wear the Rolls-Royce nameplate until the end of 2002. Present besides the three companies were the premiers of Saxony and Bavaria—the highest officials of the states where VW and BMW are headquartered.

points.h: BMW recruited shipyard and restaurant workers to hand-craft Rolls-Royce cars
points.body: BMW's new factory was sited in Goodwood, which had traditions in shipbuilding, furniture, and saddlery craftsmanship. It hired skilled woodworkers and leather craftspeople from the area; even the paint shop workers were recruited from a restaurant—because restaurant staff were accustomed to rigorous cleaning protocols. Meanwhile Volkswagen stabilized Crewe's original workforce by elevating veteran engineer Gott to oversee operations, upgrading facilities, and immediately promising no layoffs—preventing BMW from poaching talent wholesale.

points.h: Both sides invested hard enough to win because they couldn't afford to lose
points.body: By 2004 Bentley sales reached 7,000 units; by 2006 they crossed 10,000—it had never sold more than 2,000 in a year before. BMW's Rolls-Royce sales also far exceeded the past, with the brand position secure. The episode argues this positive result came because both BMW and Volkswagen ‘couldn't afford to lose’—they were forced to invest enormous resources to ensure both brands succeeded, not because the acquisition was brilliantly structured. From the moment Piëch and Vickers' executives met in Churchill's lounge, a clean victory was nearly impossible.

terms.def: An offer from the buyer stating they will not increase it further and demand an immediate decision to accept or reject.

quotes.text: BMW has the capacity to build a car that matches Rolls-Royce in performance—that's no problem. But if you put a BMW badge on the front of the car, it can't fetch that price. Swap it for a Rolls-Royce badge, and you can drive the price to the heavens.
Rolls-Royce did the equivalent of swapping partners at the altar with casual ease.

If they don't consent, even if you buy the factory, the people, and the technology, you can manufacture a car that looks like Rolls-Royce—but that car cannot be called Rolls-Royce, nor can it bear the badge.

I think Volkswagen was probably betting on fait accompli—seize the factory, the technology, the people, lock them down, and then you have leverage to force them to see reason. I'm at the table now, chips are down.
What we really valued from the start was the factory and the Bentley brand. We spent the money and got what we wanted—felt it was well worth it.
